hints: Focus on what makes an alcohol secondary, think about the carbon carrying the OH group and how many other carbons it is joined to.
Start with the straight 5-carbon chain and slide the OH to the middle positions, remembering that ends give primary alcohols.
Now try the branched 4-carbon skeleton and check where the OH can sit on a carbon joined to two others to make a new, different structure.
walkthrough:
**Recall What Secondary Means**

A secondary alcohol has the OH group on a carbon that is attached to two other carbon atoms. It is not on an end carbon (that is primary) and not on a carbon with three carbon neighbours (that is tertiary).

Rule to test:
$$ \text{secondary} = \text{C(OH) bonded to 2 x C} $$

**Check The Straight-Chain Pentane Skeleton**

Draw $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and place OH in different places. Position 1 is primary, so ignore it.

Two different secondary positions remain:
$$ \text{pentan-2-ol: CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 $$
$$ \text{pentan-3-ol: CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3 $$

**Check The Branched Skeleton**

The other carbon skeleton for $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$ is 2-methylbutane. Placing OH to make a secondary alcohol gives only one new structure.

The new isomer is:
$$ \text{3-methylbutan-2-ol: CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH(OH)CH}_3 $$

**Count And Conclude**

We have 2 from the straight chain plus 1 from the branched chain. The $\text{C}_1$ skeleton with three methyl groups can only give a primary alcohol, and the other branched position gives the tertiary alcohol 2-methylbutan-2-ol.

Total structurally isomeric secondary alcohols:
$$ 2 + 1 = 3 $$

options.A: 1 is too low. It counts only one straight-chain alcohol, such as pentan-2-ol, and misses pentan-3-ol and the branched secondary alcohol.
options.B: 2 counts the two straight-chain alcohols, pentan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol, but forgets that the branched skeleton also gives a secondary alcohol, 3-methylbutan-2-ol.
options.C: 3 is correct. There are pentan-2-ol, pentan-3-ol, and 3-methylbutan-2-ol. Each has OH on a carbon bonded to two other carbons, and no other arrangement gives a new secondary structure.
options.D: 4 is too high. It usually comes from wrongly counting the tertiary isomer 2-methylbutan-2-ol as secondary, or from double-counting the same branched structure with different numbering.
